summary: Extends SIP so a client can ask that responses be sent back to the source address and port the request came from, instead of the port in the Via header. This helps when the client is behind a NAT or firewall that does not allow incoming messages to that port. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: If you send a letter from a place that only accepts replies to the door you used, you want the answer sent there. This memo lets a phone program ask for that.

questions: what is the sip rport parameter
how does sip work behind a nat
subtitle: A small Via parameter that lets a SIP client behind a NAT get responses back on the port its request came from.

tldr.problem: Over UDP, SIP sends responses to the source IP address of the request but to the port written in the topmost Via header. Behind a NAT that response does not match the binding the request created, so it never reaches the client.
tldr.mechanism: The client adds a valueless rport parameter to its topmost Via. The server fills in the real source port, adds a received parameter with the source IP address, and sends the response back to that address and port from the address and port the request arrived on.
tldr.outcome: Clients behind NATs can receive responses. The RFC also warns that using rport to learn your own address for registrations or record routing is brittle, and says better solutions are needed.

today: RFC 3581 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself says that using it to register or record-route through NATs is not appropriate and calls for better solutions.

sections.title: The Response Routing Problem
sections.content:
When SIP runs over UDP, a server returns a response to the source IP address of the request, but to the port written into the topmost Via header field value. The RFC calls this a hybrid way of computing the destination: the address comes from the IP packet headers and the port from the SIP message. SIP does this so that a server can listen for requests and responses on a single IP address and port, which helps scalability.

The hybrid breaks down when the client is behind a NAT. The response will not match the binding the NAT created for the request, so it does not traverse the NAT properly.

There is a second gap. A client can learn the source IP address the server saw from the received parameter in the response, but there is no way to learn the source port. This RFC adds a new Via parameter, rport, that fills both gaps. It is analogous to received, but carries a port number instead of an IP address.
sections.eli5: Normally the reply goes to the right building but to the wrong door. Behind a NAT, only the door you used to send the letter will let the reply in, so the reply has to go there.

sections.title: Client Behavior
sections.content:
A compliant client (UACs and proxies both count as clients) MAY include an rport parameter in the top Via header field value of requests it generates. The parameter MUST have no value. It works as a flag meaning that the client supports this extension and wants it for the transaction.

If the request goes out over UDP, the client MUST be prepared to receive the response on the same IP address and port it used as the source of the request. For backwards compatibility it MUST also still be prepared to receive a response on the port in the sent-by field of the topmost Via.

A NAT binding must survive for the whole transaction. The RFC notes that most UDP NAT bindings appear to time out after about one minute, which is longer than non-INVITE transactions. INVITE transactions can take arbitrarily long, so the client SHOULD retransmit its INVITE every 20 seconds or so, even after a provisional response. A UA MAY run the binding lifetime discovery algorithm from RFC 3489 and then adjust the retransmission interval to half of the discovered lifetime, though the RFC warns that discovery can be unreliable.
sections.eli5: The phone program raises a little flag saying 'reply to the door I am using.' While it waits for a long answer, it knocks again every 20 seconds or so so the door does not get locked.

sections.title: Server Behavior
sections.content:
When a compliant server (a proxy or UAS) receives a request, it checks the topmost Via. If that Via has an rport parameter with no value, the server MUST set it to the source port of the request. The server MUST also insert a received parameter holding the source IP address, even if that is identical to the sent-by value. This happens regardless of transport protocol.

When sending a response, the server looks at the topmost Via of the response. If the transport is unreliable unicast such as UDP, there is no maddr parameter, and there are both received and rport parameters, the response MUST go to the address in received and the port in rport. It MUST be sent from the same address and port the request was received on. The RFC says this adds a new processing step between bullets two and three in Section 18.2.2 of RFC 3261.

Sending from the same address and port is needed to traverse symmetric NATs. A server listening on several ports or interfaces must remember which one received the request. A stateful proxy can store that for the transaction. A stateless proxy cannot, so it can encode the destination address and port of the request into the Via value it inserts and read it back when the response arrives.
sections.eli5: The server writes down which door the letter came through, and sends the reply back out of its own matching door. A helper with no memory writes that note on the envelope itself.

sections.title: Syntax of rport
sections.content:
The grammar is response-port = "rport" [EQUAL 1*DIGIT]. The value is optional, which is how a client sends it as a bare flag and a server returns it with a port number.

The new element is added to the existing Via parameter alternatives, so via-params becomes via-ttl / via-maddr / via-received / via-branch / response-port / via-extension.
sections.eli5: The word 'rport' can be written alone, like a flag, or followed by a number, like a flag with a door number on it.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
A client at 10.1.1.1 sends an INVITE from source port 4540 with Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 10.1.1.1:4540;rport;branch=z9hG4bKkjshdyff. The proxy at 192.0.2.2 listens on ports 5060 and 5070, and the client sends to port 5060. A NAT on the way changes the source to 192.0.2.1, port 9988.

The proxy forwards the request after adding received=192.0.2.1 and rport=9988 to the client's Via. When the 200 OK comes back, the proxy removes its own Via, sees both parameters on the next one, and sends the response to 192.0.2.1 port 9988, from port 5060 on 192.0.2.2. That matches the NAT binding, so the NAT rewrites the destination back to 10.1.1.1 port 4540 and the client receives it.
sections.eli5: The reply goes to the outer door number the NAT assigned, and the NAT knows to carry it to the real room inside.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
With this extension, responses reveal the source port a request came from. If the source address and port are sensitive, requests SHOULD be protected with SIP over TLS. In that case the extension does no response routing, because that only applies to unreliable transports, and just tells the client the source port the server saw.

An attacker acting as a man in the middle could remove the rport parameter from a request, which would stop clients behind NATs from receiving service. Adding it generally has no impact. The RFC judges the attack not significant, since an attacker with that capability has other ways to deny service, such as discarding the request.
sections.eli5: Someone sneaky in the middle could scratch out the flag so replies get lost. But if they can do that, they could also just throw the letter away.

sections.title: IAB Considerations and Brittleness
sections.content:
The IAB studied UNSAF (Unilateral Self Address Fixing) protocols, which let a client behind a NAT learn the address and port the NAT allocates. The RFC says that although it was not designed for that, rport together with received can be used this way, so it must address the IAB's questions. Its primary purpose, receiving responses through a NAT, is not an UNSAF use.

The side uses are registrations (learning an address to put in a Contact header of a REGISTER) and record routing (placing a learned address in a Record-Route header). The SIP working group considers using this specification for those purposes inappropriate and lists problems:

  • UDP registrations must be refreshed nearly one hundred times more frequently than the typical registration refresh interval, adding load.
  • A client cannot accurately learn the NAT binding lifetime, so calls or messages may be missed.
  • With a symmetric NAT, the client can only receive requests from the server it contacted, not other servers in a cluster, and only if the server sends from the address and port it received the registration on, which RFC 3261 does not mandate.
  • If the registrar is not the server the REGISTER went to, it only works if the server uses the Path header field.

The long-term solution should not make the client specify its address, should handle server clusters, and should not increase network load. The RFC says that at the time of writing it knew of only very limited use of this specification for address fixing.
sections.eli5: Using the door-number trick to also find out your own address works a bit, but it is wobbly and needs lots of extra knocking. The authors say a sturdier fix should come later.
